title: Proving Inequalities with the MVT
quickIdea: To prove f(x) >= g(x) between two points, apply the mean value theorem to the difference and bound its derivative on the interval between them.
remember: e^x >= 1 + x for x >= 0: on [0, x] the theorem gives e^x - 1 = e^c x with 0 < c < x, and e^c >= 1.
|sin a - sin b| <= |a - b| for all a, b: the derivative cos is bounded by 1 in absolute value.
The direction of the inequality comes from the sign of b - a. On a negative interval the same bound reverses, so write the theorem as f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a) and read the signs.
The bound is sharp only where the derivative bound is attained; e^x >= 1 + x is an equality exactly at x = 0.

example.prompt: Use the mean value theorem to show that e^0.5 >= 1.5.
example.work: Apply the theorem to f(x) = e^x on [0, 0.5]: e^0.5 - e^0 = e^c (0.5 - 0) for some c in (0, 0.5). Since e^c >= 1 on that interval, e^0.5 - 1 >= 0.5.
example.answer: e^0.5 >= 1.5. Numerically e^0.5 = 1.6487, so the bound holds with room to spare.

gateAngle: No verified GATE CSE question in this topic asks for an inequality proof, which is why this card is P3. It is kept because the same one-line bound (|f'| <= M) is what the 2021 Set 2 Q.25 question uses, and because inequality statements appear as MSQ options.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Show that ln(1.5) <= 0.5 using the mean value theorem.
variations.answer: Apply the theorem to ln(1 + x) on [0, 0.5]: ln(1.5) - ln(1) = 0.5/(1 + c) <= 0.5.
variations.why: The derivative 1/(1 + c) is at most 1 because c > 0. Numerically ln(1.5) = 0.4055, which is the value the bound is protecting.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Which is larger for x > 0: e^x or 1 + x + x^2/2?
variations.why: Apply the theorem twice, or use the second-order Taylor bound with Lagrange remainder, which is the mean value theorem applied to the difference. At x = 0.5 the two sides are 1.6487 and 1.625, so the gap is real but small - a good multiple-select distractor.

trap.what: Quoting the bound without checking the sign of b - a.
trap.why: f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a); if b < a the factor is negative and the inequality flips.
trap.counterexample: The bound ln(1 + x) <= x is stated for x >= 0. At x = -0.5 the left side is ln(0.5) = -0.693 and the right side is -0.5, so the inequality is false - the interval runs the other way.

check.question: Show that |cos 1 - cos 0.5| <= 0.5.
check.answer: True, because |sin c| <= 1 for the c the theorem produces.
check.explanation: cos 1 - cos 0.5 = -sin(c)(0.5) for some c in (0.5, 1), so the absolute value is at most 0.5. Numerically cos 1 = 0.5403 and cos 0.5 = 0.8776, a difference of 0.337.
